# Part 1 {.section-title}

## How LLMs Handle Tabular Data

------------------------------------------------------------------------

## What an LLM "sees" {.slide-title}

:::: body-text
When you upload a CSV to ChatGPT:

- The file is **converted to text tokens**
- Everything the model can "know" about your data is what fits in its
  **context window**
- If your file is too large, the model **silently truncates** it

::: callout-warning
ChatGPT will **not** tell you it only read part of your dataset. It will
produce summaries that look complete.
:::
::::

------------------------------------------------------------------------

## Token Limits by Model {.slide-title}

::: body-text
| Model       | Token Limit | Approx. CSV capacity             |
|-------------|-------------|----------------------------------|
| GPT-3.5     | \~4,000     | \~200 rows × 10 cols             |
| GPT-4 (8k)  | \~8,000     | \~400 rows × 10 cols             |
| GPT-4-turbo | \~128,000   | \~6,000–10,000 rows × 10–20 cols |

Rule of thumb: **each cell ≈ 5–10 tokens**

*Today's dataset: NAPL-only fish survey subset (\<8 KB) → works fine
with free ChatGPT*
:::

------------------------------------------------------------------------

## Three Modes of LLM Data Work {.slide-title}

:::::: columns
::: {.column width="28%"}
**Interpretation**

Reads data as text, reasons in natural language

*Good for:* inspection, description

*Reliability:* moderate — verify against domain knowledge
:::

::: {.column width="28%"}
**Code Execution**

Writes & runs Python; returns real results

*Good for:* computation, visualization

*Reliability:* high *if* the code is correct
:::

::: {.column width="28%"}
**Narrative Generation**

Converts results to plain language

*Good for:* methods & results writing

*Reliability:* high for prose, lower for numerical accuracy
:::
::::::

------------------------------------------------------------------------

## The Key Skill {.slide-title}

:::: body-text
::: callout-tip
## Know which mode you're in

Each mode has different risks and needs different verification:

- **Interpretation** → compare to what you know about the data
- **Code execution** → inspect the code; re-run in R
- **Narrative** → check numbers against actual model output
:::

*Chat: Which mode do you think is most useful for your thesis research?
Post one sentence.*
::::

# Part 2 {.section-title}

## Dataset Inspection in ChatGPT

------------------------------------------------------------------------

## Our Practice Dataset {.slide-title}

::: body-text
**SBC LTER Annual Fish Survey — NAPL subset**

```         
https://sbclter.msi.ucsb.edu/external/Reef/Data/trial_data/
Annual_survey_NAPL_only.csv
```

- Download and upload via **paperclip** — not a URL link
- Start a **new chat** before uploading
- Free ChatGPT (GPT-3.5/4) works fine for this file size

*Students: you're welcome to follow along with a dataset from your own
thesis work*
:::

------------------------------------------------------------------------

## 2.1 — First Look {.slide-title}

:::: body-text
**Prompt to use:**

::: {.callout-note icon="false"}
*Tell me about this dataset. What does it appear to contain, what types
of variables are present, and what might this data be used to study?*
:::

**As you read the response, notice:**

- What ecological context did it identify without metadata?
- What did it get right? What did it oversimplify or miss?
- This is pattern recognition from training, not domain expertise
::::

------------------------------------------------------------------------

## 2.2 — Missing Values {.slide-title}

:::: body-text
**Prompt:**

::: {.callout-note icon="false"}
*Which columns contain missing values, and how many are in each column?
Present this as a table. Then tell me whether the missingness pattern
suggests data not collected versus species not observed.*
:::

**Biological interpretation matters:**

- Missing **COUNT** → species likely not observed → structural zero
- Missing **SIZE** → animal counted but not measured → different issue

These have **very different** implications for analysis
::::

------------------------------------------------------------------------

## 2.3 — Summary Statistics {.slide-title}

:::: body-text
**Prompt:**

::: {.callout-note icon="false"}
*Provide summary statistics — mean, median, standard deviation, min, max
— for the COUNT and SIZE columns. Also list unique values for SITE and
YEAR.*
:::

**Watch for:**

COUNT distribution is almost certainly **right-skewed** — mean \>\>
median because a few species dominate

This informs model family selection later *(Poisson? Negative
binomial?)*
::::

------------------------------------------------------------------------

## 2.4 — Data Transformation {.slide-title}

:::: body-text
**Prompt:**

::: {.callout-note icon="false"}
*Convert this dataset to wide format using SP_CODE as column headers and
COUNT as values. If a species appears more than once for the same site
and year combination, sum the counts. Show me the first 10 rows and tell
me the dimensions of the resulting table.*
:::

**Verify:** Row count in wide format should equal the number of unique
**site × year** combinations

*We specified what to do with duplicates — intentional. "Tell me the
dimensions" is a mini data guardian check built right into the prompt.*
::::

------------------------------------------------------------------------

# Part 3 {.section-title}

## Data Guardian Prompts

------------------------------------------------------------------------

## The Core Problem {.slide-title}

:::: body-text
::: callout-warning
## LLMs produce confident output regardless of silent failures

- A join removes 20% of your rows → well-formatted result
- A filter excludes a whole year → beautiful plot
- A model is misspecified → significant p-value
- Data was silently truncated → authoritative summary

**The model will not volunteer that anything went wrong.** You have to
ask.
:::

**Data Guardian Prompts** force the model to show its work at every step
— like controls in a lab experiment.
::::

------------------------------------------------------------------------

## The 10 Data Guardian Prompts {.slide-title}

::: body-text
| \#  | Name                        | When                               |
|-----|-----------------------------|------------------------------------|
| 1   | Data Ingestion Verification | After every upload                 |
| 2   | Row Accountability          | After every transformation         |
| 3   | Duplicate Detection         | Before aggregation or joins        |
| 4   | Join Audit                  | After every merge                  |
| 5   | Zero vs. NA Distinction     | Before count/abundance analysis    |
| 6   | Outlier Flagging            | Before fitting any model           |
| 7   | Scope Confirmation          | Before running analysis            |
| 8   | Model Assumption Check      | After fitting, before interpreting |
| 9   | Aggregation Transparency    | After any summary or plot          |
| 10  | Reproducibility Handoff     | Last thing in every session        |
:::

------------------------------------------------------------------------

## Guardian Prompt 1 {.slide-title}

### Data Ingestion Verification

:::: body-text
::: {.callout-note icon="false"}
*After loading the data, confirm: (1) the number of rows and columns,
(2) the column names and data types, (3) the first 5 rows. Do not
proceed with any analysis until you have shown me this information.*
:::

**Why:** The very first thing that can go wrong is that the model didn't
read what you think it read.

**Watch for:** Row count doesn't match your file → stop and investigate
before continuing.

**When:** Run this immediately after **every upload**.
::::

------------------------------------------------------------------------

## Guardian Prompt 2 {.slide-title}

### Row Accountability After Every Transformation

:::: body-text
::: {.callout-note icon="false"}
*After each data transformation step, print the row count and the count
of any NA or zero values in the key response variable. If any
transformation removes rows, stop and report which rows were removed and
why before continuing.*
:::

**Why:** Filtering, joining, dropping NAs, pivoting — any of these can
remove rows without warning.

**Watch for:** LLMs tend to pipeline steps together. Push back — ask for
counts after **each individual step**.
::::

------------------------------------------------------------------------

## Guardian Prompt 3 {.slide-title}

### Duplicate Detection Before Aggregation

:::: body-text
::: {.callout-note icon="false"}
*Before performing any aggregation or join, check whether there are
duplicate rows based on the key columns \[list them\]. Report the number
of duplicate groups and show me 3 example duplicate records. Do not
aggregate until I confirm the duplicates are expected.*
:::

**Why:** Undetected duplicates inflate counts and means. One species
appearing twice in the same site-year inflates trend estimates —
invisibly.

**Note:** Confirming **absence** of duplicates is as valuable as
detecting presence.
::::

------------------------------------------------------------------------

## Guardian Prompt 4 {.slide-title}

### Join Audit

:::: body-text
::: {.callout-note icon="false"}
*After performing the join, report: (1) the row count of each input
table, (2) the row count of the result, (3) any keys present in one
table but not the other. If the result has more rows than the larger
input, explain why.*
:::

**Why:** Inner joins silently drop unmatched rows. Left joins can
inflate rows if the right table has duplicates.

**Rule:** Result rows \> larger input rows → many-to-many duplication.
Investigate immediately.
::::

------------------------------------------------------------------------

## Guardian Prompt 5 {.slide-title}

### Zero vs. NA — Force Explicit Distinction

:::: body-text
::: {.callout-note icon="false"}
*Before any analysis involving COUNT or abundance: distinguish between
cells where the value is 0 (species observed but none counted) and cells
where the value is NA (data not collected). Report the count of each. Do
not treat zeros and NAs as equivalent in any analysis.*
:::

**Why:** In ecological count data, 0 and NA have fundamentally different
biological meanings. Models that conflate them — or drop both — produce
wrong answers.

**Especially critical for:** zero-inflated models, occupancy analyses,
species distribution models.
::::

------------------------------------------------------------------------

## Guardian Prompt 6 {.slide-title}

### Outlier Flagging Before Modeling

:::: body-text
::: {.callout-note icon="false"}
*Before fitting any model, identify values in \[response variable\] that
are more than 3 standard deviations from the mean. List them with their
row identifiers and ask me whether to include, exclude, or investigate
them before proceeding.*
:::

**Why:** Outliers can dominate regression results. The model will fit
whatever you ask for regardless of whether one record is driving the
entire trend estimate.

**Important:** Do NOT automatically exclude outliers — in ecology,
extreme values are often real and ecologically meaningful. Surface them
for **your judgment**.
::::

------------------------------------------------------------------------

## Guardian Prompt 7 {.slide-title}

### Scope Confirmation

:::: body-text
::: {.callout-note icon="false"}
*Before running any analysis, restate in plain language: (1) which rows
are included (what filters have been applied), (2) which columns are
used, and (3) what the analysis unit is. Confirm this matches my
research question.*
:::

**Why:** After multiple transformation steps, it's easy to lose track of
what subset the analysis is actually running on.

**Key move:** If the model's restatement doesn't match your intent,
correct it **before** it runs anything. Far easier than diagnosing a
wrong answer afterward.
::::

------------------------------------------------------------------------

## Guardian Prompt 8 {.slide-title}

### Model Assumption Check Before Interpretation

:::: body-text
::: {.callout-note icon="false"}
*After fitting the model, check and report: (1) residual deviance and
degrees of freedom, (2) whether the dispersion parameter suggests
overdispersion, (3) a residual plot, and (4) influential observations.
Do not present conclusions until these checks are done.*
:::

**Why:** A Poisson GLM with overdispersion produces standard errors that
are too small and p-values that are too significant — and the model will
show them with full confidence regardless.

**Rule of thumb:** deviance/df \> 2 → switch to negative binomial.
::::

------------------------------------------------------------------------

## Guardian Prompt 9 {.slide-title}

### Aggregation Transparency

:::: body-text
::: {.callout-note icon="false"}
*When you aggregate or summarize this data, tell me: (1) how many
original rows contributed to each summary value, (2) what function was
used (sum, mean, median), and (3) whether any rows were excluded and
why.*
:::

**Why:** Every time series plot involves aggregation. Making the model
describe the operation lets you verify the plot shows what you think it
shows.

**Watch for:** Whether NAs were excluded or treated as zero before
aggregation — default behavior varies by language and function.
::::

------------------------------------------------------------------------

## Guardian Prompt 10 {.slide-title}

### Reproducibility Handoff

:::: body-text
::: {.callout-note icon="false"}
*Please compile all the code used in this session into a single,
self-contained R script that I can run locally. The script should load
the data from file, reproduce every transformation and visualization we
discussed, and include comments explaining each step. List any steps
performed in Python that will need translation to R.*
:::

**Why:** Analysis done inside ChatGPT is ephemeral. This prompt converts
a session into a permanent, auditable record.

**Run it as the last thing you do in every session.** Then verify the
script in RStudio.
::::

------------------------------------------------------------------------

## Deploying the Prompts {.slide-title}

::: body-text
You don't have to use all 10 every time

Think of them as **targeted controls** — deploy at the moments when
silent errors are most likely:

- **Uploads** → Prompt 1
- **Each wrangling step** → Prompt 2
- **Before any join or aggregation** → Prompts 3, 4, 9
- **Count/abundance data** → Prompt 5
- **Before modeling** → Prompts 6, 7
- **After fitting** → Prompt 8
- **End of session** → Prompt 10

*Chat: Which one do you think you'd be most likely to forget to use on
your own data? Why?*
:::

------------------------------------------------------------------------

# Part 4 {.section-title}

## Statistical Analysis in ChatGPT

------------------------------------------------------------------------

## Setting Up: Scope First {.slide-title}

:::: body-text
Before any plots or models, deploy **Guardian Prompt 7**:

::: {.callout-note icon="false"}
*Before creating any plots: restate which rows are included in the
analysis, what the analysis unit is, and whether NA values in COUNT have
been handled.*
:::

This confirms we all agree on what data we're working with before the
analysis begins.

*Continue in the same chat from Part 2.*
::::

------------------------------------------------------------------------

## 4.1 — Time Series: Total Count {.slide-title}

:::: body-text
**Prompt with Guardian Prompt 9 built in:**

::: {.callout-note icon="false"}
*Create a time series plot of total fish count across all species, with
YEAR on the x-axis and total COUNT on the y-axis. Use different colors
for each SITE. After creating the plot, tell me how many rows
contributed to each year's total and whether any years had missing
data.*
:::

**Watch:** Are all sites represented in every year? Year-to-year
variability vs. directional trend?
::::

------------------------------------------------------------------------

## 4.2 — Top Species Composition {.slide-title}

:::: body-text
**Prompt:**

::: {.callout-note icon="false"}
*Create a time series plot of the top 5 most abundant species across all
years. Before plotting, report which 5 species were selected and their
total counts so I can verify the ranking.*
:::

**"Before plotting, report..."** is the key move — it surfaces the
intermediate aggregation step before the visualization obscures it.

If the top 5 don't match your ecological expectation, you catch it
**here** — not after the plot is in your paper.
::::

------------------------------------------------------------------------

## 4.3 — Model Selection Consultation {.slide-title}

:::: body-text
**Prompt with Guardian Prompt 8 pre-flight:**

::: {.callout-note icon="false"}
*I want to understand whether total fish count has increased or
decreased over time. Before recommending a model, tell me: (1) whether
count data with many zeros is appropriate for a Poisson GLM or whether
another family is more suitable, and (2) what assumptions that model
makes that I should verify.*
:::

**Listen for the reasoning chain:**

Count data → Poisson → check equidispersion → many zeros →
zero-inflation risk → variance \> mean → overdispersion → consider
negative binomial
::::

------------------------------------------------------------------------

## 4.4 — Fitting and Checking the Model {.slide-title}

:::: body-text
**Prompt:**

::: {.callout-note icon="false"}
*Fit a Poisson GLM with total annual count as the response and YEAR as
the predictor. After fitting, report: (1) residual deviance and degrees
of freedom, (2) the dispersion ratio (deviance/df), (3) whether this
suggests we should switch to a negative binomial model. Do not interpret
results until after this check.*
:::

"Do not interpret until after this check" is doing a lot of work — the
LLM's natural tendency is to move directly to interpretation. We're
**interrupting that flow deliberately**.
::::

------------------------------------------------------------------------

## Reading the Dispersion Check {.slide-title}

::::::: body-text
::::: columns
::: {.column width="50%"}
**If deviance/df ≈ 1**

Poisson is appropriate — proceed with interpretation
:::

::: {.column width="50%"}
**If deviance/df \> 2**

Overdispersion detected → refit with negative binomial

Standard errors from Poisson will be too small → p-values will be too
significant
:::
:::::

**Follow-up if needed:**

::: {.callout-note icon="false"}
*The dispersion ratio suggests overdispersion. Please refit using a
negative binomial GLM, then show me the coefficient for YEAR and its 95%
confidence interval. Interpret in plain language — what does it mean for
how fish counts change per year?*
:::
:::::::

------------------------------------------------------------------------

## 4.5 — Report-Ready Narrative {.slide-title}

:::: body-text
**Prompt:**

::: {.callout-note icon="false"}
*Write a methods and results paragraph suitable for a scientific report
describing the GLM analysis. Include the model family and link function,
the reason for choosing it, the key statistical results (coefficient,
confidence interval, p-value), and a plain-language interpretation of
the trend. Use past tense and avoid jargon where possible.*
:::

This is one of ChatGPT's **strongest capabilities** — the paragraph will
be close to publication-ready.

**Critical read:** Does the narrative accurately reflect the model you
*actually* fitted? Narrative quality is not evidence that the numbers
are right.
::::

------------------------------------------------------------------------

# Part 5 {.section-title}

## Reproducibility: Export & Verify in R

------------------------------------------------------------------------

## The Problem {.slide-title}

:::: body-text
::: callout-warning
## Everything we just did exists only in this chat window

- Close the tab → it's gone
- Screenshot → not reproducible
- The analysis cannot be peer-reviewed, shared, or built upon
:::

This is not a hypothetical concern — it's the default state of any
ChatGPT data analysis session.

**The fix:** Guardian Prompt 10 — every time.
::::

------------------------------------------------------------------------

## Send the Reproducibility Handoff {.slide-title}

:::: body-text
**Guardian Prompt 10 in the chat:**

::: {.callout-note icon="false"}
*Please compile all the code used in this session into a single,
self-contained R script that I can run locally. The script should: load
the data from file, reproduce every transformation and visualization we
discussed, and include comments explaining each step. After generating
the script, list any steps performed in Python that will need
translation to R.*
:::

Copy the R script → paste into RStudio → **run it**.
::::

------------------------------------------------------------------------

## What to Verify {.slide-title}

::::::: body-text
When running the exported script, check:

::::: columns
::: {.column width="50%"}
**Numbers**

- Row counts match what ChatGPT reported?
- GLM coefficients match?
- p-values match?
:::

::: {.column width="50%"}
**Structure**

- All packages available?
- Data loads from file correctly?
- Transformations produce same dimensions?
:::
:::::

::: callout-warning
Any numerical discrepancy in coefficients or row counts is a **bug to
resolve** — not a rounding difference to ignore.
:::
:::::::

------------------------------------------------------------------------

## A Reusable Verification Pattern {.slide-title}

::: body-text
Paste this helper into any R script after ChatGPT exports:

```{r}
#| eval: false
verify_step <- function(df, label, response_col) {
  cat("\n---", label, "---\n")
  cat("  Rows:", nrow(df), "\n")
  cat("  NAs in", response_col, ":",
      sum(is.na(df[[response_col]])), "\n")
  cat("  Zeros in", response_col, ":",
      sum(df[[response_col]] == 0, na.rm = TRUE), "\n")
}

# Use after every transformation:
# verify_step(fish, "after loading", "COUNT")
# verify_step(fish_clean, "after dropping NAs", "COUNT")
```

This is Guardian Prompt 2 implemented as reusable R code.
:::

------------------------------------------------------------------------

# Wrap-Up {.section-title}

------------------------------------------------------------------------

## The Reliability Landscape {.slide-title}

:::::: body-text
::::: columns
::: {.column width="50%"}
**Where LLMs are genuinely strong**

- First-look data description
- Generating plausible analysis options
- Writing methods & results prose
- Translating between R and Python
- Explaining statistical reasoning
:::

::: {.column width="50%"}
**Where silent failure is common**

- Large datasets (truncation)
- Multi-step transformations
- Joins across tables
- Zero vs. NA handling
- Model assumption checking
- Any result you don't independently verify
:::
:::::
::::::

------------------------------------------------------------------------

## The Core Principle {.slide-title}

:::: body-text
::: callout-important
## Data Guardian Prompts don't make the LLM smarter

They force it to **show its work** so that *you* can catch the errors.

The LLM will produce confident, well-formatted output regardless of
whether it is computing on the right data, the right subset, or using
the right model.

**You are always the last line of defense.**
:::
::::
